newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugo analysts disagree on exchange rate policy.
newsitem.headline: Yugo analysts disagree on exchange rate policy.

text.p: The International Monetary Fund is likely ask Yugoslavia to introduce a floating exchange rate as its key precondition for normalising relations, economists say.
Although they have widely agreed the fixed rate would have to go, there was a disagreement about whether a devaluation should follow.

"A stubborn maintainance of the (existing) fixed exchange rate is unrealistic," said the leading analyst at the Institute of Economic Sciences Stojan Stamenkovic. "There is no doubt about the need for a floating exchange rate."
"The IMF will insist that the government change the exchange rate policy as one of the main preconditions for talks on the first stand-by arrangement (with the fund)."
According to a survey by the Institute for Market Research, Yugoslav exporters would rather see the local currency dinar devalued.
Exporters argue that would help them return to foreign markets and reverse the trade deficit which surged to one billion dollars in the first seven months of the year.
"With a policy of fixed exchange rate imposed by our former central bank governor we cannot improve our results," said one exporter who asked not to be named. "We need a weaker dinar."
But Stamenkovic was resolute that devaluation should not even be discussed: "It is out of the question."
Stamenkovic conceeded high inflation that reached 99.2 percent in the year to August gave exporters a case to argue.
"But the black market exchange rate, formed on the basis of supply and demand, does not support the (exporters') argument," he said.
The black market exchange rate -- considered a reflection of the dinar's true value -- is stable at 3.4 to the German mark, less than 10 percent off the official rate of 3.3 dinars.
The former central bank governor Dragoslav Avramovic, known for curbing country's 1993 hyperinflation, devalued the dinar by 70 percent last November bringing it into line with the black market rate.
Zivojin Jevtic of the Belgrade-based Foreign Trade Research Institute believes devaluation is inevitable if the government can not reign in inflation.
He argued that inflation was already putting pressure on the dinar's current rate, but said that any devaluation would help to blow out the already massive trade deficit.
But a federal government official talking under condition of anonimity warned that devaluation could plunge the economy back into a vicious inflationary cycle.
"The problem is that we do not have a person of Avramovic's authority and credibility (with the public) who would dare to devalue dinar."
"Psychologicaly it would be bad as we are the country with a high inflatory expectations," the official said. "And that would take us back into a vicious circle again."
A central bank official who also asked not to be named agreed that the fixed exchange rate helped stabilise prices and control inflatory expectations in the past.
"But now our policy of fixed exchange rate must change," he said. "However I do not expect anything to happen before the year end."
